newsitem.title: USA: Kmart says can add up to $10 billion in sales.
newsitem.headline: Kmart says can add up to $10 billion in sales.

text.p: Kmart Corp. Chairman Floyd Hall predicted Tuesday that the retailer can boost sales from its more than 2,000 discount stores by as much as $10 billion in 1997 without adding new outlets.
But Hall acknowledged at Kmart's annual shareholder meeting the company has made mistakes with in some key product lines such as women's clothing and still needs to improve.

Slow sales of women's and men's clothing left Kmart with about $100 million in excess inventory in its first quarter, and Hall said after the meeting that Kmart will use markdowns to clear that inventory in the second quarter.
"We think we can manage our way out of that," Hall said. "We do have some markdown liability there."

Troy, Mich.-based Kmart, the nation's third largest discount retailer, had total sales of $31.4 billion in 1996, down from $31.7 billion. Net income from continuing operations was $231 million, compared with a loss of $230 million.

Citing the company's 1996 operating performance -- its strongest annual results since 1992 -- Hall painted a picture of a company on the road to recovery. But he said the company has much work to do. Kmart's $201 in sales per square foot trail the $386 for industry leader Wal-Mart Stores Inc. and $270 for Dayton Hudson Corp.'s Target Stores.
"At the top of our agenda in 1997 is a tenacious push toward growing sales and improving profitability," Hall said.
He said the company plans to introduce a new Sesame Street line of clothing for infants, toddlers, boys and girls, as well as toys, books and related products this summer.
Within three months, Kmart will announce "state-of-the-art" initiatives that will improve service and convenience for shoppers, he said.

After its unsuccessful restaurant venture last year, Kmart has brought in new executives to run its in-store restaurants itself. Under the new "KCafe" concept, Kmart has cut the size of the restaurants in half.

This week it is rolling out a new "co-branded" programme for its 850 in-store restaurants. The new restaurants will have expanded menu offerings that feature national brands such as Ball Park Franks and Little Caesars pizza.

Compared to previous years, Hall faced a generally friendly audience of shareholders and employees. One of the exceptions was Chinese human rights activist Harry Wu. Wu accused Kmart of violating its own policies by buying 73 tons of men's rainwear and ponchos last fall from a company controlled by Chinese military officials.
"Kmart should be ashamed that it is subsidising Chinese political commissars and strengthening oppression in China," Wu said.

Kmart officials said they would look into the charges, which they said they were unaware of until Tuesday. However, Wu produced a May 1994 letter from a Kmart executive denying that it does business with the "People's Liberation Army."
Kmart spokeswoman Shawn Kahle said the company would remove the products from its stores if the charges are true.
